issue: Added interpretive claim not in source: candidate "would work against the public good in such a case" (source only says the love of fame, which would prompt a man to plan great undertakings if he could finish them, "would, on the contrary, deter him"). Neutral lead-in substituted; the following two sentences already carry the contrast.
replacement: One bad effect of the exclusion would be a reduction of the inducements to good behavior. There are few men who would not feel much less zeal in the discharge of a duty when they knew that the advantages of the position connected with it must be given up at a fixed time, than when they were allowed to hope to earn a continuance of those advantages by deserving it. This point will not be disputed, so long as it is admitted that the desire of reward is one of the strongest incentives of human conduct, or that the best security for the fidelity of mankind is to make their interests coincide with their duty. Even the love of fame, the ruling passion of the noblest minds, would be affected in such a case. If a man could flatter himself with the prospect of being allowed to finish what he had begun, that passion would prompt him to plan and undertake extensive and arduous enterprises for the public benefit, enterprises requiring considerable time to mature and perfect. But when he foresaw that he must leave the scene before he could accomplish the work, and must commit it, together with his own reputation, to hands that might be unequal or unfriendly to the task, that same passion would deter him from the undertaking. The most that can be expected from the generality of men in such a situation is the negative merit of doing no harm, in place of the positive merit of doing good.

issue: "sensible to the apprehension of suspicion or censure" means responsive to the fear of it; candidate "less aware of the danger of suspicion or censure" shifts the sense from feeling the fear to merely knowing of a danger.
replacement: He is also to be authorized to grant "reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment." Humanity and sound policy join in dictating that the merciful prerogative of pardoning should be as little restricted or hampered as possible. The criminal code of every country has so much necessary severity in it that, without easy access to exceptions in favor of unfortunate guilt, justice would wear a face too bloody and cruel. The sense of responsibility is always strongest in proportion as it is undivided. It may therefore be inferred that a single man would be most ready to attend to the force of those motives that might plead for a softening of the rigor of the law, and least likely to yield to considerations meant to shelter a fit object of its vengeance. The thought that the fate of a fellow creature depended on his sole decision would naturally inspire scrupulousness and caution. The dread of being accused of weakness or connivance would produce an equal circumspection, though of a different kind. On the other hand, since men generally draw confidence from their numbers, they might often encourage one another in an act of hardness, and might be less affected by the fear of suspicion or censure for an unwise or affected clemency. For these reasons, one man appears to be a better dispenser of the mercy of government than a body of men.

issue: Source "the ministerial servant of the Senate"; candidate "the Senate's own hired agent" adds "hired" (a payment relationship the source does not state). Use "subordinate agent" (ministerial = acting under another's direction).
replacement: Entrusting the power of making treaties to the Senate alone would have meant giving up the benefit of the President's constitutional agency in conducting foreign negotiations. True, the Senate would then be free to employ him in that role, but it would be equally free to leave him out, and pique or intrigue might lead it to choose the second course rather than the first. Besides this, the Senate's own subordinate agent could not be expected to enjoy the confidence and respect of foreign powers to the same degree as the constitutional representatives of the nation, and so could not act with the same weight or effectiveness. On this account the Union would lose a considerable advantage in managing its external concerns, and the people would lose the added security that would come from the Executive's cooperation. It would be imprudent to confide so important a trust to him alone, but there can be no doubt that his participation would materially add to the safety of the society. It must indeed be clear to a demonstration that the joint possession of the power in question by the President and the Senate would offer better prospects of security than possession by either of them separately. And anyone who has carefully weighed the circumstances that must come together in the appointment of a President will be satisfied that the office will always be likely to be filled by men whose character makes their concurrence in the making of treaties especially desirable, for their wisdom as well as their integrity.

issue: Source: "The only remaining powers of the Executive are comprehended in giving information ...". Candidate "The Executive's remaining powers are all of this kind" has no antecedent for "this kind" and drops "only"; the list that follows is the content, not a "kind".
replacement: The only remaining powers of the Executive are these. He gives Congress information on the state of the Union and recommends to its consideration the measures he judges expedient. He may convene Congress, or either house, on extraordinary occasions, and he may adjourn them when they cannot agree among themselves on a time. He receives ambassadors and other public ministers, sees that the laws are faithfully executed, and commissions all the officers of the United States.

issue: Source "for if we attend carefully to its operation, it will be found..." gives the reason for "arbitrary disposition"; candidate drops the connective "for" (STYLE-NOTE: keep logical connectives).
replacement: On the intermixture of powers, I shall rely on the explanations already given elsewhere of the true meaning of the rule on which that objection rests. I shall take it for granted, as an inference from them, that joining the Executive with the Senate in the matter of treaties breaks no such rule. I venture to add that the particular nature of the power of making treaties shows a special propriety in that union. Several writers on government place that power among the executive authorities, but this is plainly an arbitrary classification, for if we look carefully at how it operates, it will be found to have more of the legislative character than of the executive, although it does not seem to fall strictly within the definition of either. The essence of legislative authority is to enact laws, that is, to prescribe rules for regulating the society. The execution of the laws, and the use of the common strength for that purpose or for the common defense, seem to make up all the functions of the chief executive. The power of making treaties is plainly neither of these. It has nothing to do with executing the existing laws, or with enacting new ones, and still less with exerting the common strength. Its objects are CONTRACTS with foreign nations, which have the force of law but get that force from the obligations of good faith. They are not rules laid down by the sovereign for the subject, but agreements between sovereign and sovereign. The power in question therefore seems to form a distinct department, belonging properly neither to the legislative nor to the executive. The qualities I detailed elsewhere as indispensable in managing foreign negotiations point to the Executive as the fittest agent in those transactions. Yet the vast importance of the trust, and the fact that treaties operate as laws, argue strongly for the participation of the whole legislative body, or a part of it, in the business of making them.
